title: Computer games for Preschoolers Nintendo's Research and Design Process
sourceHeading: Computer Games for Preschoolers: Nintendo’s Research and Design Process

source.filename: Practice 47  IETLS 閱讀練習 - Passage 1.pdf

paragraphs.text: Designing computer games for young children is a daunting task for game producers, who for a long time concentrated on more ‘hard-core’ game enthusiasts. This article chronicles the design process and research involved in creating Nintendo DS games for preschoolers.

After speaking with producers who had a keen interest in designing for the DS, we agreed on three key goals. The first was to understand the range of preschoolers’ physical and cognitive abilities in the context of gameplay on a handheld system. The second was to understand how preschoolers interacted with the DS, particularly how they controlled the forms of play and game mechanics offered by products already on the market. The third was to understand parents’ expectations of handheld systems, as well as the purchasing and gameplay contexts in which they were used. The research team decided that in-home ethnographic studies with preschoolers and their families would yield a comprehensive body of data for the producers. We therefore began by conducting 26 such studies in three markets across the United States: an urban and suburban area on the East Coast, one on the West Coast, and a suburban and rural area in the Midwest.

The participants included 15 girls and 11 boys, ranging in age from 3 years and 3 months to 5 years and 11 months. Because earlier research had shown that older siblings affected gameplay—for example, children with older siblings displayed more advanced motor coordination when using a computer mouse—we selected households that included preschoolers both with and without older siblings. To study both experienced and new users of the platform, we divided the sample so that 13 families owned at least one Nintendo DS and the remainder did not. A DS was brought to each interview in a household that did not own one so the child could play. This allowed us to observe the instinctive movements of new players, and of experienced players trying unfamiliar games, as well as the learned movements of experienced users. Each interview lasted approximately 60 to 120 minutes and included the preschooler, at least one parent, and often siblings or another caregiver.

Three kinds of information were collected during each interview. From available parents and older siblings, we gathered data about decisions to buy game systems, the family’s typical gameplay patterns, levels of parental moderation of computer gaming, and family members’ favourite games. The in-home interviews also helped us understand each household’s approach to gaming: the spaces used for gameplay, how systems were installed, where handheld play occurred both at home and on the move, and the number and types of games and game systems owned. Most importantly, we collected gameplay information for every child.

Before conducting the interviews, the research team consulted the in-house game producers to create a list of game mechanics and potential problems associated with preschoolers’ motor and cognitive abilities that needed to be understood before the games were written. These ranged from general dexterity issues involving controllers to the effectiveness of in-game instructions and specific mechanics in existing games that the producers wanted to implement in future preschool titles. During the interviews, the moderator guided each preschooler through a series of games, observed the interaction, and asked both the child and the parents about feelings, attitudes and frustrations that arose in different situations.

If a participant had previously used the DS, he or she was first asked to play a favourite game on it. This gave researchers information about the child’s current level of skill relative to the chosen game’s complexity and allowed them to observe familiar mechanics. Across the 26 preschoolers, the range of Nintendo DS games selected was broad and included New Super Mario Bros., Sonic Rush, Nintendogs and Tony Hawk’s Proving Ground. The interviewer observed the child playing, noting preferences for game mechanics, motor interactions with the device and the level of complexity each mechanic presented. In consultation with the producers, the researchers also asked every preschooler to play The Little Mermaid: Ariel’s Undersea Adventure. The game was chosen for two main reasons. First, it was one of the few on the market with characters that appealed to this young age group. Second, it incorporated a wide variety of mechanics unique to the DS platform, including use of the microphone for blowing or singing.

The findings from this initial study were extensive. After reviewing the results and discussing their implications with our internal production team, we outlined the design requirements and presented them to a firm specialising in game design. We worked closely with its experts to base the design of two preschool-oriented DS games then in development on what we had learnt.

As the two DS games entered development, a formative research process was established. Whenever we developed new game mechanics, we brought preschoolers into our in-house usability laboratory to test them and assess both their simplicity and their appeal. We tested alpha or beta versions of individual game elements as well as the overall game structure. Once a full version of each DS game was ready, we returned to the field and tested it with twelve preschoolers and their parents. This ensured that every game element worked for the children, the overall objective was understandable and the experience was enjoyable. We also collected parents’ feedback on whether they considered the game appropriate, engaging and worth purchasing.
